Positive electrode — negative ions lose electrons (oxidation)
Ionic compound in solution or molten that conducts electricity
Breakdown of an ionic compound using electricity

question: Match each term to its correct definition in terms of electron transfer.

pairs.definition: Substance that accepts electrons and is itself reduced
Substance that donates electrons and is itself oxidised

question: Match each metal to its correct position in the reactivity series (most to least reactive).

pairs.definition: Most reactive — reacts vigorously with water
Moderately reactive — reacts slowly with dilute acids
Less reactive than zinc — used in construction

question: State the ion produced by all acids in aqueous solution.
mark_scheme: Hydrogen ion / H⁺ (1).

question: State what OIL RIG stands for.
mark_scheme: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons) (1).

question: Define the term oxidation in terms of electrons.
mark_scheme: Oxidation is the loss of electrons (1).

question: State what happens to positive ions during electrolysis.
mark_scheme: Positive ions move to the cathode (negative electrode) where they gain electrons and are reduced (1).

question: Describe what is observed when excess copper oxide is added to warm dilute sulfuric acid.
mark_scheme: Black copper oxide dissolves (1); blue solution forms (copper sulfate solution) (1); excess black powder remains undissolved (1) — any two.

question: Explain why copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid but zinc does.
mark_scheme: Zinc is higher than hydrogen in the reactivity series so can displace hydrogen from the acid (1); copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series so cannot displace it (1).

question: Explain why an ionic compound must be molten or in solution for electrolysis to occur.
mark_scheme: In solid form ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move (1); when molten or dissolved, ions are free to move to the electrodes (1).

question: Write a word equation for the reaction between magnesium and sulfuric acid.
mark_scheme: Magnesium + sulfuric acid → magnesium sulfate + hydrogen (1); correct reactants and products (1).

question: Explain the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid of the same concentration.
mark_scheme: Strong acid fully ionises in water, releasing all H⁺ ions (1); weak acid only partially ionises, fewer H⁺ ions in solution / higher pH (1).

question: Describe what is produced at each electrode during the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid.
mark_scheme: Hydrogen gas produced at the cathode (1); oxygen gas produced at the anode (1).

question: In the displacement reaction between zinc and copper sulfate solution, identify which species is oxidised and which is reduced. Explain your answer.
mark_scheme: Zinc is oxidised — it loses electrons to form Zn²⁺ (1); Cu²⁺ ions are reduced — they gain electrons to form copper metal (1).

question: State two metals that are extracted from their ores by electrolysis and explain why this method is used.
mark_scheme: Any two from: aluminium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, potassium (1); these metals are above carbon in the reactivity series so cannot be reduced by carbon (1).

question: Explain how electrolysis is used to extract aluminium from aluminium oxide.
mark_scheme: Aluminium oxide is melted to free the ions (1); electricity is passed through the molten electrolyte (1); Al³⁺ ions move to the cathode and gain electrons to form aluminium metal (1); oxide ions move to the anode and lose electrons, forming oxygen gas (1) — any three.

question: Describe how a pure, dry sample of copper sulfate could be made from copper oxide and sulfuric acid.
mark_scheme: Add excess copper oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid and stir (1); filter to remove excess copper oxide (1); evaporate the solution to crystallise the copper sulfate / leave to cool and filter crystals (1).

question: Explain how the reactivity series can be used to predict whether a displacement reaction will occur. Give an example.
mark_scheme: A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt (1); the more reactive metal takes the place of the less reactive one (1); e.g. zinc added to copper sulfate solution — zinc displaces copper as zinc is more reactive (1).

question: Explain the process of electrolysis of molten lead bromide. Include what happens at each electrode and the half equations for each reaction.
mark_scheme: Lead bromide melted so ions free to move (1); Pb²⁺ ions move to cathode and are reduced: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb (1); Br⁻ ions move to anode and are oxidised: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (1); lead metal produced at cathode, bromine gas at anode (1).

question: Describe how to prepare a pure dry sample of zinc sulfate from zinc carbonate and sulfuric acid. Include all practical steps.
mark_scheme: Add excess zinc carbonate to dilute sulfuric acid — effervescence indicates reaction (1); filter off excess zinc carbonate (1); heat the filtrate gently to evaporate water and concentrate the solution (1); leave to cool and crystallise, filter and dry the crystals (1).

question: Explain what happens in a redox reaction. Use the reaction between magnesium and oxygen as an example, identifying what is oxidised and reduced.
mark_scheme: Redox involves simultaneous oxidation and reduction (1); 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO (1); magnesium is oxidised — loses electrons to form Mg²⁺ (1); oxygen is reduced — gains electrons to form O²⁻ (1).

question: Evaluate the use of electrolysis as a method for extracting metals. Include advantages, disadvantages, and state which metals require this method.
mark_scheme: Metals above carbon in reactivity series (e.g. aluminium, sodium) must be extracted by electrolysis (1); advantage: only method available for highly reactive metals (1); disadvantage: requires large amounts of electrical energy — expensive and high carbon footprint (1); less reactive metals e.g. iron extracted more cheaply by reduction with carbon in a blast furnace (1).

question: Explain the difference between strong and weak acids. Include reference to ionisation, pH, and give an example of each. Explain how the concentration and strength of an acid are different concepts.
mark_scheme: Strong acid fully ionises in water — all H⁺ ions released e.g. HCl (1); weak acid partially ionises — few H⁺ ions released e.g. ethanoic acid (1); same concentration: strong acid has lower pH than weak acid (1); concentration refers to amount of acid per dm³ — can have concentrated weak acid or dilute strong acid (1); strength and concentration are independent — both affect pH (1).

question: Evaluate how the reactivity series is used in the extraction of metals from their ores. Discuss the methods used for different metals and the economic and environmental considerations.
mark_scheme: Most reactive metals (above carbon) extracted by electrolysis e.g. aluminium (1); less reactive metals (below carbon) extracted by reduction with carbon e.g. iron in blast furnace (1); least reactive metals (e.g. gold, silver) found uncombined / native (1); electrolysis is expensive due to high energy costs (1); reduction with carbon is cheaper but releases CO₂ contributing to climate change (1); economic and environmental trade-offs must be considered — e.g. aluminium is expensive but very useful / recyclable (1).

question: Explain how electrolysis of brine (concentrated sodium chloride solution) is used in industry. State what is produced at each electrode, give the half equations, and describe two industrial uses of the products.
mark_scheme: Brine is concentrated NaCl solution (1); at cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ — hydrogen gas produced (1); at anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ — chlorine gas produced (1); sodium hydroxide solution remains (1); use of chlorine: making bleach / PVC / disinfecting water (1); use of hydrogen: making margarine / ammonia (Haber process) / fuel cells (1).

question: Explain the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid. Include what happens when each dissolves in water and how pH relates to hydrogen ion concentration.
mark_scheme: Strong acid: fully dissociates in water — all molecules ionise to produce H⁺ ions (1); weak acid: partially dissociates — equilibrium between ionised and un-ionised forms (1); same concentration: strong acid has lower pH — more H⁺ ions (1); pH decreases as H⁺ concentration increases — pH = −log[H⁺] (1).

question: Describe how to prepare a pure, dry sample of copper sulfate crystals by reacting copper oxide with sulfuric acid.
mark_scheme: Add excess copper oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid (1); stir until no more dissolves — excess solid shows acid is neutralised (1); filter to remove excess copper oxide (1); evaporate solution to concentrate, then allow to crystallise; filter and dry crystals (1).

question: Explain why gold is found as a pure element in the Earth's crust while iron must be extracted from its ore. Refer to the reactivity series.
mark_scheme: Gold is very unreactive — low in the reactivity series (1); does not react with oxygen or water — remains as pure metal (1); iron is more reactive — reacts with oxygen to form iron(III) oxide ore (haematite) (1); more reactive metals form stable compounds with non-metals — require more energy/chemical methods to extract (1).

question: Explain what is meant by oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer. Use the reaction between zinc and copper sulfate as an example.
mark_scheme: Oxidation: loss of electrons; reduction: gain of electrons — OIL RIG (1); Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu (1); zinc is oxidised: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (loses electrons) (1); copper ions are reduced: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (gains electrons) (1).

question: Describe what happens at each electrode during the electrolysis of molten lead bromide. Include the half-equations.
mark_scheme: Lead bromide melted — ions free to move (1); cathode (negative): Pb²⁺ ions attracted, gain electrons — lead metal deposited: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb (1); anode (positive): Br⁻ ions attracted, lose electrons — bromine gas produced: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (1); lead and bromine are the products of electrolysis (1).

question: Explain what a neutralisation reaction is. Write a balanced equation for the reaction of sodium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid. Include the ionic equation.
mark_scheme: Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water (1); NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O (1); ionic equation: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O (1); the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions — not involved in the reaction (1).

question: Describe how the products of electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride differ from electrolysis of molten sodium chloride. Explain why the products differ.
mark_scheme: Molten NaCl: Na metal at cathode, Cl₂ gas at anode (1); aqueous NaCl: H₂ gas at cathode (not Na), Cl₂ at anode (1); in aqueous solution: water provides H⁺ and OH⁻ ions as well (1); H⁺ ions discharged in preference to Na⁺ at cathode — H⁺ more easily reduced (lower in reactivity series) (1).

question: Evaluate the industrial extraction of aluminium by electrolysis. Explain why electrolysis is needed and one disadvantage of this method.
mark_scheme: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series — too reactive to be reduced by carbon (1); electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (bauxite) is used (1); Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al at cathode (1); disadvantage: very high energy cost — aluminium oxide has high melting point (~2000°C); electrolysis uses large amounts of electricity (1).

question: Explain what is meant by a displacement reaction in terms of redox. Use the reaction between iron and copper sulfate solution as an example.
mark_scheme: In a displacement reaction, a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound (1); Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (1); iron is oxidised: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (1); copper ions are reduced: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu — copper deposited on iron (1).

question: Describe the method for preparing an insoluble salt by precipitation. Use barium sulfate as an example.
mark_scheme: Mix two soluble salt solutions — one containing Ba²⁺ ions and one containing SO₄²⁻ ions (1); e.g. barium chloride + sodium sulfate solutions (1); BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄↓ + 2NaCl — precipitate forms immediately (1); filter to collect solid, wash with distilled water, dry (1).

question: Explain the difference between the reactions of metals with dilute acids and their reactions with water. Give an example of a metal that reacts with water but not vigorously with acid.
mark_scheme: Metals react with dilute acids to produce salt + hydrogen: Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂ (1); reaction with water produces metal hydroxide + hydrogen (1); metals high in reactivity series (Na, K) react vigorously with water — may not react with acid safely (1); e.g. sodium: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ — reacts violently; reaction with acid would be explosive (1).

question: Explain the industrial electrolysis of brine (sodium chloride solution). Include the products at each electrode and their industrial uses.
mark_scheme: Brine = aqueous NaCl — contains Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺, OH⁻ ions (1); cathode: H⁺ discharged in preference to Na⁺ — hydrogen gas produced: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (1); anode: Cl⁻ discharged in preference to OH⁻ — chlorine gas: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (1); remaining solution: NaOH (sodium hydroxide) (1); uses: H₂ → fuel/margarine; Cl₂ → bleach/PVC/water treatment; NaOH → soap/paper manufacture (1).

question: Evaluate the use of displacement reactions to extract metals from their ores. Include examples and compare with electrolysis.
mark_scheme: Carbon reduction: iron ore (Fe₂O₃) + carbon → iron + CO₂ — carbon displaces iron (1); used for metals below carbon in reactivity series (Fe, Cu, Pb, Sn) (1); cheaper than electrolysis — carbon (coke) is inexpensive (1); electrolysis needed for metals above carbon (Al, Na) — too reactive for carbon reduction (1); electrolysis: more expensive due to electricity costs, but only method available for reactive metals (1).

question: Describe how to measure the pH of solutions using universal indicator and a pH meter. Include the advantages of each method and give examples of pH values for common substances.
mark_scheme: Universal indicator: add a few drops to solution — compare colour to chart; gives approximate pH (1); pH meter: calibrated with buffer solutions; probe placed in solution — gives precise numerical pH (1); pH meter more accurate — gives reading to 1 or 2 decimal places (1); UI useful for quick, rough measurement; pH meter better for lab investigations (1); examples: HCl pH~1, vinegar pH~3, water pH=7, NaOH pH~13 (1).

question: Explain how the reactivity series of metals was established experimentally. Include reactions with oxygen, water, and acid.
mark_scheme: Metals reacted with oxygen: those that burn brightly are more reactive (e.g. Mg burns vigorously, gold doesn't react) (1); reactions with water: potassium reacts explosively, sodium vigorously, calcium steadily — more reactive = faster reaction (1); reactions with dilute acid: magnesium reacts rapidly, zinc slowly, copper doesn't react (1); displacement reactions: more reactive metals displace less reactive from salt solutions (1); combining all evidence gives ordered reactivity series: K>Na>Ca>Mg>Al>Zn>Fe>Sn>Pb>Cu>Ag>Au (1).

question: Evaluate the use of copper plating by electrolysis for industrial applications. Include how copper plating works and why it is used.
mark_scheme: Copper plating: object to be plated is cathode, copper anode, copper sulfate solution as electrolyte (1); Cu²⁺ ions deposited on cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (1); copper anode dissolves to replenish Cu²⁺ ions: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (1); uses: decorative coating on jewellery/trophies (1); protects against corrosion; PCB circuit manufacture; electroforming complex shapes (1).

question: Explain how to predict the solubility of ionic compounds and which salts are insoluble. Include solubility rules and an example of preparing an insoluble salt.
mark_scheme: All sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble (1); all nitrates are soluble (1); most chlorides are soluble except silver and lead chloride (1); most sulfates are soluble except barium, lead and calcium sulfate (1); preparation of insoluble salt: mix solutions containing the required ions — precipitate forms; filter, wash, dry (e.g. AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO₃) (1).

question: Describe the reactions of acids with metals, metal oxides, metal hydroxides and metal carbonates. Include the products in each case.
mark_scheme: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂ (1); metal oxide + acid → salt + water: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O (1); metal hydroxide + acid → salt + water: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O (1); metal carbonate + acid → salt + water + CO₂: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ (1); in all cases acid is neutralised — H⁺ ions react (1).

question: Explain the terms oxidising agent and reducing agent. Use the thermite reaction between aluminium and iron(III) oxide as an example.
mark_scheme: Oxidising agent: substance that oxidises another — gains electrons itself (is reduced) (1); reducing agent: substance that reduces another — loses electrons itself (is oxidised) (1); thermite reaction: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe (1); aluminium is the reducing agent — reduces iron oxide to iron; Al → Al³⁺ (oxidised) (1); Fe₂O₃ is the oxidising agent — oxidises aluminium; Fe³⁺ → Fe (reduced) (1).

question: Evaluate different methods for producing soluble and insoluble salts. Include direct acid-base neutralisation, precipitation and titration.
mark_scheme: Soluble salts from acid + base: use excess solid base then filter — simple but requires care (1); acid + alkali titration: gives accurate quantities but product must be crystallised (1); precipitation: for insoluble salts — mix two solutions; rapid and simple (1); quality considerations: crystallisation gives pure product; precipitation may have impurities from residual ions (1); choice depends on solubility of desired product and available reagents (1).

question: Explain the electrolysis of aqueous copper sulfate using copper electrodes, compared with inert (graphite) electrodes. Include the electrode reactions in both cases.
mark_scheme: With graphite electrodes: cathode — Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (copper deposited) (1); anode — 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ (oxygen gas, water oxidised) (1); concentration of CuSO₄ decreases over time as Cu²⁺ used up (1); with copper electrodes: cathode reaction same — copper deposited (1); anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ — copper anode dissolves, replenishes Cu²⁺ (1); concentration of CuSO₄ stays constant; net transfer of copper from anode to cathode — used in copper purification (1).

question: Evaluate the extraction methods used for copper, aluminium and iron. Include the method, why it is used, and its economic and environmental impact.
mark_scheme: Iron: blast furnace, carbon reduction — iron ore + coke + limestone → iron + CO₂ + slag (1); suitable because iron is below carbon in reactivity series; CO₂ released contributes to climate change (1); aluminium: electrolysis of molten bauxite (Al₂O₃) — needed as Al above carbon (1); very high energy use — large electricity cost and carbon footprint unless renewable energy used (1); copper: smelting and electrolytic refining — or phytomining/bioleaching for low-grade ores (1); traditional smelting releases SO₂; phytomining more sustainable but slower (1).

question: Explain the concept of acid-base reactions in terms of proton transfer (Brønsted-Lowry theory). Include conjugate acid-base pairs and apply this to the reaction of ammonia with water.
mark_scheme: Brønsted-Lowry: acid = proton (H⁺) donor; base = proton acceptor (1); NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ (1); NH₃ acts as a base — accepts H⁺ from water to form NH₄⁺ (1); H₂O acts as acid — donates H⁺ to ammonia (1); conjugate pairs: NH₃/NH₄⁺ and H₂O/OH⁻ (1); reaction is reversible — NH₄⁺ can donate H⁺ back (conjugate acid acts as acid in reverse reaction) (1).

question: Describe the redox reactions involved in the blast furnace extraction of iron. Include the role of coke, limestone, and hot air, and write the equations at each stage.
mark_scheme: Coke (carbon) burns with hot air: C + O₂ → CO₂ (1); CO₂ then reduced by more coke: CO₂ + C → 2CO (carbon monoxide formed) (1); CO reduces iron ore: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ — carbon monoxide is reducing agent (1); Fe is reduced (gains electrons): Fe³⁺ → Fe (1); limestone decomposes: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (1); CaO reacts with silica impurity: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (slag) — removes acidic impurities (1).

question: A student wants to make a pure, dry sample of zinc sulfate. Evaluate two different methods they could use: reacting zinc with dilute sulfuric acid, and reacting zinc oxide with dilute sulfuric acid. Include advantages and disadvantages of each.
mark_scheme: Method 1 — Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂: advantages: straightforward, uses cheap reagents (1); disadvantages: hydrogen gas produced — safety concern (1); may be slow; zinc must be in excess to ensure all acid consumed; harder to filter (unreacted zinc vs. zinc sulfate solution) (1); Method 2 — ZnO + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂O: safer — no gas produced (1); excess ZnO easy to filter off — leaves pure ZnSO₄ solution (1); evaporate and crystallise to get solid ZnSO₄·7H₂O — preferred method (1).

question: Explain oxidation states and use them to identify which elements are oxidised and reduced in the reaction: MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ (in acid solution). Include half-equations.
mark_scheme: Oxidation state rules: O = −2, overall charge = sum of oxidation states (1); in MnO₄⁻: Mn oxidation state = +7 (1); Mn goes from +7 to +2 — decreases by 5 — Mn is reduced (1); Fe goes from +2 to +3 — increases by 1 — Fe is oxidised (1); half-equations: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (reduction) (1); Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (oxidation) — multiply by 5 and combine (1).

question: Explain what is meant by a buffer solution. Describe how an ethanoic acid / sodium ethanoate buffer resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added.
mark_scheme: Buffer: a solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added (1); weak acid (CH₃COOH) and its conjugate base (CH₃COO⁻) present in solution (1); add acid: H⁺ ions react with CH₃COO⁻ — equilibrium shifts left, H⁺ absorbed (1); add alkali: OH⁻ reacts with CH₃COOH — equilibrium shifts right, OH⁻ absorbed (1); pH remains approximately constant — important in blood (pH 7.35–7.45) (1).

question: Evaluate the use of fuel cells as an alternative to combustion engines. Include the redox reactions involved and compare in terms of efficiency and environmental impact.
mark_scheme: Hydrogen fuel cell: H₂ oxidised at anode: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ (1); O₂ reduced at cathode: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O (1); produces only water — no CO₂ emissions at point of use (1); more efficient than combustion — converts chemical energy directly to electrical energy (1); limitation: hydrogen production currently mainly from natural gas (SMR) — releases CO₂; storage and infrastructure challenges (1).

question: Describe the industrial manufacture of nitric acid from ammonia (Ostwald process). Include all stages, conditions, and the redox chemistry involved.
mark_scheme: Stage 1: catalytic oxidation of ammonia — 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O; platinum/rhodium catalyst, 900°C (1); ammonia is oxidised: N goes from −3 to +2 (1); Stage 2: oxidation of NO to NO₂ — 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ (1); Stage 3: absorption of NO₂ in water — 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO (1); NO recycled back to Stage 2 — improves efficiency (1); product is ~60% nitric acid — concentrated by distillation; used to make fertilisers (ammonium nitrate) and explosives (1).

question: Evaluate electrolysis as a method for the industrial production of chemicals. Include the production of aluminium, chlorine and sodium hydroxide. Consider energy costs and benefits to society.
mark_scheme: Aluminium: electrolysis of molten cryolite/Al₂O₃ — only method for this reactive metal (1); very high energy use — aluminium recycling saves 95% of energy (1); chlorine: from brine electrolysis — essential for PVC, bleach, water purification (1); sodium hydroxide co-produced — used in soap, paper, food processing (1); hydrogen co-produced — potential clean fuel (1); environmental concerns: large electricity consumption; if from fossil fuels adds to CO₂ emissions; industrial scale benefits society through materials/chemicals (1).
